expectedText:
CONTROLLING SHAREHOLDER FIDUCIARY DUTY TO MINORITY SHAREHOLDERS — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme Widgets, Inc.

PURPOSE AND SCOPE — CONTROLLING SHAREHOLDER FIDUCIARY DUTY INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet relates to Acme Widgets, Inc., a corporation organized under the laws of California, and to Jordan Lee's status as a shareholder of Acme Widgets, Inc. It describes the fiduciary duty that California case law imposes on majority or controlling shareholders of a corporation toward the minority shareholders and the corporation itself — the rule announced by the California Supreme Court in Jones v. H. F. Ahmanson & Co. (1969) 1 Cal.3d 93 — together with the "inherent fairness" standard that accompanies it, the distinction the same decision drew between a minority shareholder's individual claim and a derivative claim brought on the corporation's behalf, later Court of Appeal decisions applying that distinction, and the statutory backdrop in Corporations Code §§ 309 and 1800. Transaction or conduct this information sheet may relate to, if applicable: officer compensation increases approved by the two majority shareholders.

This information sheet is about the duty owed by those who control a corporation through their share ownership, acting singly or together. It is distinct from several other documents in this project: the Director's Duty of Care and the Business Judgment Rule document, which covers the standard of conduct Corporations Code § 309 sets for directors as such; the Self-Dealing and Interested Director/Officer Transactions document, which covers the statutory approval procedures of Corporations Code § 310; the Shareholder Derivative Lawsuit document, which covers the procedural conditions Corporations Code § 800 places on suits brought in the corporation's right; the Involuntary Dissolution of a Corporation document, which covers the dissolution remedy of Corporations Code §§ 1800-1809 in depth; and the LLC Member and Manager Fiduciary Duties document, which covers the statutory duties of Corporations Code § 17704.09 for limited liability companies rather than corporations.

This information sheet is educational only. It does not itself constitute a complaint, a demand, or any other filing; does not determine whether any person is a "controlling" shareholder of Acme Widgets, Inc., whether any particular transaction or course of conduct breached a duty described below, whether a claim would be individual or derivative in character, or what remedy, if any, a court would order; and does not constitute legal advice.

THE RULE: MAJORITY OR CONTROLLING SHAREHOLDERS OWE A FIDUCIARY DUTY TO THE MINORITY AND THE CORPORATION
In Jones v. H. F. Ahmanson & Co. (1969) 1 Cal.3d 93, the California Supreme Court rejected the defendants' position that shareholders, as shareholders, owe no fiduciary obligation to other shareholders absent reliance on inside information, use of corporate assets, or fraud — describing that view as one "long been repudiated in California." The court stated the governing rule in two parts. First, majority shareholders, whether acting singly or in concert to accomplish a joint purpose, have a fiduciary responsibility both to the minority and to the corporation to use their ability to control the corporation in a fair, just, and equitable manner. Second, majority shareholders may not use their power to control corporate activities to benefit themselves alone or in a manner detrimental to the minority; any use to which they put the corporation, or their power to control it, must benefit all shareholders proportionately and must not conflict with the proper conduct of the corporation's business. The opinion uses the terms "majority" and "controlling" shareholders interchangeably in stating the duty, and frames it as a duty arising from the ability to control the corporation. Later published Court of Appeal decisions — Jara v. Suprema Meats, Inc. (2004) 121 Cal.App.4th 1238 and Sheley v. Harrop (2017) 9 Cal.App.5th 1147 — quote and apply this same formulation as the settled statement of the duty, with Jara observing that the parties before it did not question "the basic principle of the fiduciary duty owed by majority shareholders to minority shareholders."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "The Courts of Appeal have often recognized that majority shareholders, either singly or acting in concert to accomplish a joint purpose, have a fiduciary responsibility to the minority and to the corporation to use their ability to control the corporation in a fair, just, and equitable manner."
  — Jones v. H. F. Ahmanson & Co., 1 Cal.3d 93, 108 (Cal. 1969) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1123091/jones-v-h-f-ahmanson-co/)
  "Majority shareholders may not use their power to control corporate activities to benefit themselves alone or in a manner detrimental to the minority. Any use to which they put the corporation or their power to control the corporation must benefit all shareholders proportionately and must not conflict with the proper conduct of the corporation's business."
  — Jones v. H. F. Ahmanson & Co., 1 Cal.3d 93, 108 (Cal. 1969) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1123091/jones-v-h-f-ahmanson-co/)
  "The parties do not question the basic principle of the fiduciary duty owed by majority shareholders to minority shareholders."
  — Jara v. Suprema Meats, Inc., 121 Cal.App.4th 1238, 1252 (Cal. Ct. App. 2004) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2259573/jara-v-suprema-meats-inc/)
  "It is clear that, under the circumstances at issue here, and based on the admissible materials submitted by respondent, appellants owed respondent a fiduciary duty in their capacities as majority shareholders and directors of the corporation."
  — Sheley v. Harrop, 9 Cal.App.5th 1147, 1171 (Cal. Ct. App. 2017) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/4376881/sheley-v-harrop/)
  Known gap: This rule is case law; no California statute states a general fiduciary duty of controlling shareholders as such (Corporations Code § 309 addresses directors, and § 310 addresses interested-director transactions). The two Court of Appeal decisions cited here quote Jones's formulation verbatim rather than independently restating it, so they corroborate that the Jones formulation remains the operative rule but are not independent sources for its wording. Jones itself cites earlier Court of Appeal decisions (Brown v. Halbert, Burt v. Irvine Co., Efron v. Kalmanovitz, and Remillard Brick Co. v. Remillard-Dandini Co.) as the origin of the rule; those underlying decisions were not independently fetched or re-verified for this document. Jones does not define a numerical threshold for "control": the defendants there held a majority (later 85 to 87 percent) of the shares, and the opinion does not decide whether or when a holder of less than a majority may be a controlling shareholder. This document does not determine whether any specific shareholder of any specific corporation holds control within the meaning of this rule.

THE STANDARD: A COMPREHENSIVE RULE OF "INHERENT FAIRNESS"
Jones describes the standard that has developed in California as "a comprehensive rule of 'inherent fairness from the viewpoint of the corporation and those interested therein,'" quoting the Court of Appeal's earlier decision in Remillard Brick Co. v. Remillard-Dandini Co. (1952) 109 Cal.App.2d 405. Jones reproduces at length the passage from Remillard — itself quoting the United States Supreme Court's decision in Pepper v. Litton — that the Court of Appeal had declared to be "the law of California": a dominant or controlling stockholder or group of stockholders, like a director, is a fiduciary whose powers are powers of trust; their dealings with the corporation are subjected to rigorous scrutiny; where any of their contracts or engagements with the corporation is challenged, the burden is on the director or stockholder not only to prove the good faith of the transaction but also to show its inherent fairness from the viewpoint of the corporation and those interested in it; and the essence of the test is whether, under all the circumstances, the transaction carries the earmarks of an arm's length bargain, failing which equity will set it aside. Jones adds that Remillard "clearly indicated that the fiduciary obligations of directors and shareholders are neither limited to specific statutory duties and avoidance of fraudulent practices nor are they owed solely to the corporation to the exclusion of other shareholders."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "The rule that has developed in California is a comprehensive rule of "inherent fairness from the viewpoint of the corporation and those interested therein.""
  — Jones v. H. F. Ahmanson & Co., 1 Cal.3d 93, 110 (Cal. 1969) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1123091/jones-v-h-f-ahmanson-co/)
  "Their dealings with the corporation are subjected to rigorous scrutiny and where any of their contracts or engagements with the corporation is challenged the burden is on the director or stockholder not only to prove the good faith of the transaction but also to show its inherent fairness from the viewpoint of the corporation and those interested therein"
  — Jones v. H. F. Ahmanson & Co., 1 Cal.3d 93, 108 (Cal. 1969) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1123091/jones-v-h-f-ahmanson-co/)
  "The essence of the test is whether or not under all the circumstances the transaction carries the earmarks of an arm's length bargain. If it does not, equity will set it aside."
  — Jones v. H. F. Ahmanson & Co., 1 Cal.3d 93, 108 (Cal. 1969) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1123091/jones-v-h-f-ahmanson-co/)
  "In Remillard the Court of Appeal clearly indicated that the fiduciary obligations of directors and shareholders are neither limited to specific statutory duties and avoidance of fraudulent practices nor are they owed solely to the corporation to the exclusion of other shareholders."
  — Jones v. H. F. Ahmanson & Co., 1 Cal.3d 93, 109 (Cal. 1969) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1123091/jones-v-h-f-ahmanson-co/)
  Known gap: The burden-of-proof and "arm's length bargain" language is Jones quoting Remillard, which was in turn quoting Pepper v. Litton (1939) 308 U.S. 295, a federal bankruptcy decision; Jones adopts it by reproducing it with approval, but the words originate in that chain of quotation rather than in the Jones court's own drafting. Neither Remillard nor Pepper v. Litton was independently fetched for this document; the quotations are taken from Jones's reproduction of them. In the CourtListener text of Jones the quoted passage is interspersed with bracketed headnote numbers such as "(9)" and "(10)" inserted by the reporter; the quotations below omit those numbers and reproduce only the opinion's own words between them. How the burden of proof operates in any particular procedural posture, and what evidence would satisfy it, are questions beyond what the quoted text resolves and are not addressed by this document.

SCOPE: EXERCISE OF CORPORATE POWERS, STATUTORY POWERS, AND DEALINGS IN THE CONTROLLING BLOCK ITSELF
Jones states that the inherent-fairness rule "applies alike to officers, directors, and controlling shareholders in the exercise of powers that are theirs by virtue of their position and to transactions wherein controlling shareholders seek to gain an advantage in the sale or transfer or use of their controlling block of shares." Two consequences follow in the opinion. First, powers that a statute ostensibly grants to majority shareholders remain subject to equitable limitations in favor of the minority: Jones recounts the court's earlier holding in In re Security Finance Co. (1957) 49 Cal.2d 370 that majority shareholders do not have an absolute right to dissolve a corporation, even though the then-governing statute permitted a majority to do so, because that statutory power is subject to equitable limitations — the majority could dissolve to protect their investment only if no alternative means were available and no advantage was secured over other shareholders. Second, the duty reaches a controlling shareholder's dealings in its own shares, not only its votes and management of the corporation: the opinion rejects the defendants' argument that in the use of their own shares they owed no duty to the minority, and holds that a sale or exchange of a controlling block is subject to close scrutiny — where the majority receives a premium over market value for its shares, the consideration for which that premium is paid will be examined, and if it reflects payment for what is properly a corporate asset, all shareholders may demand to share proportionately. Jones also observes that the traditional theories had failed to afford adequate protection to minority shareholders, "particularly to those in closely held corporations whose disadvantageous and often precarious position renders them particularly vulnerable to the vagaries of the majority."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "The rule applies alike to officers, directors, and controlling shareholders in the exercise of powers that are theirs by virtue of their position and to transactions wherein controlling shareholders seek to gain an advantage in the sale or transfer or use of their controlling block of shares."
  — Jones v. H. F. Ahmanson & Co., 1 Cal.3d 93, 110 (Cal. 1969) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1123091/jones-v-h-f-ahmanson-co/)
  "that majority shareholders do not have an absolute right to dissolve a corporation, although ostensibly permitted to do so by Corporations Code section 4600, because their statutory power is subject to equitable limitations in favor of the minority."
  — Jones v. H. F. Ahmanson & Co., 1 Cal.3d 93, 110 (Cal. 1969) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1123091/jones-v-h-f-ahmanson-co/)
  "Although a controlling shareholder who sells or exchanges his shares is not under an obligation to obtain for the minority the consideration that he receives in all cases, when he does sell or exchange his shares the transaction is subject to close scrutiny. When the majority receives a premium over market value for its shares, the consideration for which that premium is paid will be examined. If it reflects payment for that which is properly a corporate asset all shareholders may demand to share proportionately."
  — Jones v. H. F. Ahmanson & Co., 1 Cal.3d 93, 117 (Cal. 1969) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1123091/jones-v-h-f-ahmanson-co/)
  "These theories have failed to afford adequate protection to minority shareholders and particularly to those in closely held corporations whose disadvantageous and often precarious position renders them particularly vulnerable to the vagaries of the majority."
  — Jones v. H. F. Ahmanson & Co., 1 Cal.3d 93, 111 (Cal. 1969) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1123091/jones-v-h-f-ahmanson-co/)
  Known gap: The In re Security Finance Co. holding is described here as Jones summarizes it; that 1957 decision was not independently fetched, and the dissolution statute it construed (former Corporations Code § 4600) has since been replaced by the current General Corporation Law (Corporations Code §§ 1900 et seq. and 1800 et seq.), so the specific statutory reference in the quotation is historical. Jones states that a controlling shareholder who sells or exchanges shares "is not under an obligation to obtain for the minority the consideration that he receives in all cases," so the premium-sharing principle is stated as a matter of scrutiny of the particular consideration, not as a flat rule that every control premium must be shared; the opinion does not set out a test for when consideration "reflects payment for that which is properly a corporate asset." This document does not evaluate any specific sale, transfer, dissolution, or other exercise of control.

WHAT JONES HELD ON ITS FACTS: USING CONTROL TO BUILD A MARKET FOR THE MAJORITY ALONE
The Jones plaintiff owned 25 of the 6,568 outstanding shares of a California savings and loan association whose stock had no public market. The majority shareholders formed a holding company, exchanged their association shares for holding-company shares without offering the minority the same opportunity, took the holding company public — with a large part of the offering proceeds returned to themselves as capital — and pledged the association's assets and earnings to secure debt incurred for their own benefit; the association then curtailed extra dividends and the holding company offered to exchange the minority's shares on terms far below what the majority had received. On those alleged facts, the court held that the complaint stated a cause of action for breach of the majority's fiduciary duty. The court was explicit about the limits of its holding: it did not suggest that corporate fiduciaries are obligated in all cases to make a market for the corporation's stock, but held that where no market exists, controlling shareholders may not use their control for the purpose of promoting a marketing scheme that benefits themselves alone to the detriment of the minority. Nor did the court suggest that a control block may not be sold or transferred to a holding company; it decided only that the circumstances of any transfer of controlling shares are subject to judicial scrutiny when it appears the controlling shareholders may have breached their fiduciary obligation to the corporation or the remaining shareholders. The opinion notes that alternatives were available to the defendants that would have benefited all stockholders proportionately.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "In so holding we do not suggest that the duties of corporate fiduciaries include in all cases an obligation to make a market for and to facilitate public trading in the stock of the corporation. But when, as here, no market exists, the controlling shareholders may not use their power to control the corporation for the purpose of promoting a marketing scheme that benefits themselves alone to the detriment of the minority."
  — Jones v. H. F. Ahmanson & Co., 1 Cal.3d 93, 115 (Cal. 1969) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1123091/jones-v-h-f-ahmanson-co/)
  "Nor do we suggest that a control block of shares may not be sold or transferred to a holding company. We decide only that the circumstances of any transfer of controlling shares will be subject to judicial scrutiny when it appears that the controlling shareholders may have breached their fiduciary obligation to the corporation or the remaining shareholders."
  — Jones v. H. F. Ahmanson & Co., 1 Cal.3d 93, 115 (Cal. 1969) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1123091/jones-v-h-f-ahmanson-co/)
  "Alternatives were available to them that would have benefited all stockholders proportionately."
  — Jones v. H. F. Ahmanson & Co., 1 Cal.3d 93, 115 (Cal. 1969) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1123091/jones-v-h-f-ahmanson-co/)
  Known gap: Jones was decided on demurrer — the court held that the allegations, together with stipulated facts, stated a cause of action and reversed the judgment of dismissal; it did not find, after trial, that any defendant had in fact breached a duty. The factual summary above is drawn from the opinion's own recitation of the pleaded and stipulated facts. The court's statements that it "do[es] not suggest" a general market-making duty or a bar on transferring control blocks are express limits on the holding, so the case does not establish that every holding-company reorganization or every exclusion of minority holders from a transaction breaches the duty. This document does not compare the Jones facts to any specific corporation's circumstances.

INDIVIDUAL CLAIM OR DERIVATIVE CLAIM: THE JONES "GRAVAMEN OF THE COMPLAINT" TEST
Before reaching the merits, Jones addressed whether a minority shareholder complaining of the majority's conduct must sue derivatively — in the corporation's right, subject to the procedural conditions that govern derivative suits — or may sue in her own name. The court adopted a test keyed to the gravamen of the complaint: an action is derivative if the gravamen is injury to the corporation, or to the whole body of its stock and property without any severance or distribution among individual holders, or if it seeks to recover assets for the corporation or to prevent the dissipation of its assets. By contrast, a shareholder's individual suit enforces a right the shareholder possesses as an individual. Applying that test, the court held the Jones plaintiff's claim was individual: although she alleged that the value of her stock had been diminished, she did not contend that the diminished value reflected an injury to the corporation, so the gravamen of her claim was injury to herself and the other minority stockholders. The court disapproved the earlier Court of Appeal rule of Shaw v. Empire Savings & Loan Assn. that an individual action required an injury different from that suffered by other minority shareholders, holding that the individual wrong need not be unique to the plaintiff, that the same injury may affect a substantial number of shareholders, and that an individual cause of action exists if the injury is not incidental to an injury to the corporation.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "the action is derivative, i.e., in the corporate right, if the gravamen of the complaint is injury to the corporation, or to the whole body of its stock and property without any severance or distribution among individual holders, or it seeks to recover assets for the corporation or to prevent the dissipation of its assets."
  — Jones v. H. F. Ahmanson & Co., 1 Cal.3d 93, 106 (Cal. 1969) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1123091/jones-v-h-f-ahmanson-co/)
  "Although she does allege that the value of her stock has been diminished by defendants' actions, she does not contend that the diminished value reflects an injury to the corporation and resultant depreciation in the value of the stock. Thus the gravamen of her cause of action is injury to herself and the other minority stockholders."
  — Jones v. H. F. Ahmanson & Co., 1 Cal.3d 93, 107 (Cal. 1969) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1123091/jones-v-h-f-ahmanson-co/)
  "The individual wrong necessary to support a suit by a shareholder need not be unique to that plaintiff."
  — Jones v. H. F. Ahmanson & Co., 1 Cal.3d 93, 107 (Cal. 1969) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1123091/jones-v-h-f-ahmanson-co/)
  "The same injury may affect a substantial number of shareholders. If the injury is not incidential to an injury to the corporation, an individual cause of action exists."
  — Jones v. H. F. Ahmanson & Co., 1 Cal.3d 93, 107 (Cal. 1969) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1123091/jones-v-h-f-ahmanson-co/)
  Known gap: The procedural conditions on derivative suits (contemporaneous share ownership, pre-suit demand on the board or its excuse, and the security-for-costs motion) are in Corporations Code § 800 and are covered by this project's Shareholder Derivative Lawsuit document; Jones itself referred to the analogous provision then governing savings and loan associations (former Financial Code § 7616). The CourtListener text of Jones at the passage quoted below reads "incidential" rather than "incidental"; that spelling is reproduced verbatim in the quotation because it is what the fetched source contains, and appears to be a typographical artifact of the reporter or transcription rather than a difference in meaning — the official reporter text was not separately checked. The gravamen test is a characterization exercise applied to particular allegations, and this document does not characterize any specific claim as individual or derivative.

APPLYING THE TEST: DISPROPORTIONATE PROFIT-TAKING (INDIVIDUAL) VERSUS MISMANAGEMENT (DERIVATIVE)
In Jara v. Suprema Meats, Inc. (2004) 121 Cal.App.4th 1238, the Court of Appeal applied the Jones test to a three-shareholder corporation in which the two majority shareholders, who were also its only officers and directors, paid themselves compensation the minority shareholder alleged was excessive. The trial court had treated the claim as one for injury to the corporation that could be pursued only derivatively. The Court of Appeal reversed. Surveying the post-Jones decisions, it read Jones as allowing a minority shareholder to bring a personal action alleging that the majority's breach of fiduciary duty resulted in the majority retaining a disproportionate share of the corporation's ongoing value, and found that the gravamen of the plaintiff's complaint — that he was deprived of a fair share of the corporation's profits by the defendants' generous payment of executive compensation to themselves, which one defendant conceded was done to reduce the profit that had to be shared with the plaintiff — was an injury to him as an individual. The court also explained why the policies behind requiring a derivative action (avoiding multiple suits and unequal treatment of shareholders, encouraging intracorporate resolution, and protecting creditors) had little or no application where there was only one minority shareholder, the defendants were the entire board and all the officers, and the corporation remained a viable business. Jara contrasted this with mismanagement claims: it described Nelson v. Anderson (1999) 72 Cal.App.4th 111, a two-shareholder corporation, as holding that the minority shareholder had no standing to sue the majority shareholder for mismanagement, which had to be pursued through a derivative action.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "The gravamen of Jara, Sr.’s complaint is that he was deprived of a fair share of the corporation’s profits as a result of defendants’ generous payment of executive compensation to themselves. As Rodriguez conceded on cross-examination, the corporation paid bonuses to defendants with the objective of reducing the amount of profit in the corporation that had to be shared with Jara, Sr. These payments gave rise to an injury to Jara, Sr., as an individual."
  — Jara v. Suprema Meats, Inc., 121 Cal.App.4th 1238, 1258 (Cal. Ct. App. 2004) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2259573/jara-v-suprema-meats-inc/)
  "The objective of preventing a multiplicity of lawsuits and assuring equal treatment for all aggrieved shareholders does not arise at all when there is only one minority shareholder. The objective of encouraging intracorporate resolution of disputes and protecting managerial freedom is entirely meaningless where the defendants constitute the entire complement of the board of directors and all the corporate officers."
  — Jara v. Suprema Meats, Inc., 121 Cal.App.4th 1238, 1259 (Cal. Ct. App. 2004) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2259573/jara-v-suprema-meats-inc/)
  "We see nothing in Jones that bars Jara, Sr., from bringing an individual action claiming damages for the breach of fiduciary duty of majority shareholders as alleged in the second cause of action."
  — Jara v. Suprema Meats, Inc., 121 Cal.App.4th 1238, 1259 (Cal. Ct. App. 2004) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2259573/jara-v-suprema-meats-inc/)
  "Nevertheless, the court held that the minority shareholder had no standing to sue the majority shareholder for mismanagement of the corporation; the corporation itself had to bring the action through a derivative action."
  — Jara v. Suprema Meats, Inc., 121 Cal.App.4th 1238, 1255 (Cal. Ct. App. 2004) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2259573/jara-v-suprema-meats-inc/)

(1975) 47 Cal.App.3d 75 as "questionable authority" because it relied on the Shaw rule Jones disapproved; the individual-versus-derivative line therefore depends on the character of the specific allegations, and Jara itself called its facts "a closer case than Jones" on possible injury to the corporation. Jara's account of Nelson v. Anderson is quoted here as Jara's own description; Nelson was not independently fetched for this document. Jara did not decide whether the compensation at issue was in fact excessive or whether the defendants had breached their duty — the trial court had made no findings on those questions, and the Court of Appeal reversed and remanded. This document does not characterize any specific compensation, distribution, or management decision.

ELEMENTS OF THE CLAIM, AND THE SEPARATE STATUTORY DUTY WHEN CONTROLLING SHAREHOLDERS ARE ALSO DIRECTORS
In Sheley v. Harrop (2017) 9 Cal.App.5th 1147, a 25-percent shareholder cross-complained against the two shareholders who together held the other 75 percent and served as the corporation's directors. The Court of Appeal, restating the general elements, identified a claim for breach of fiduciary duty as requiring (1) the existence of a fiduciary relationship, (2) breach of the duty, and (3) damages. On the first element, the court found — quoting the Jones formulation by way of Jara — that the appellants owed the respondent a fiduciary duty in their capacities as majority shareholders and directors of the corporation. The decision illustrates that when the same persons hold a controlling block and also sit on the board, two distinct sources of duty operate at once: the case-law duty of controlling shareholders described in this information sheet, and the statutory standard of conduct for directors in Corporations Code § 309(a), which requires a director to perform the duties of a director in good faith, in a manner the director believes to be in the best interests of the corporation and its shareholders, and with the care, including reasonable inquiry, that an ordinarily prudent person in a like position would use under similar circumstances.

  "The elements of a cause of action for breach of fiduciary duty are (1) the existence of a fiduciary relationship; (2) breach of fiduciary duty; and (3) damages."
  — Sheley v. Harrop, 9 Cal.App.5th 1147, 1171 (Cal. Ct. App. 2017) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/4376881/sheley-v-harrop/)
  "It is clear that, under the circumstances at issue here, and based on the admissible materials submitted by respondent, appellants owed respondent a fiduciary duty in their capacities as majority shareholders and directors of the corporation."
  — Sheley v. Harrop, 9 Cal.App.5th 1147, 1171 (Cal. Ct. App. 2017) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/4376881/sheley-v-harrop/)

  Known gap: Sheley arose on a special motion to strike under the anti-SLAPP statute (Code Civ. Proc. § 425.16), and much of the opinion concerns which of the respondent's allegations arose from protected petitioning activity; on the fiduciary-duty claim the court ultimately held that the respondent had not shown a probability of prevailing on the specific theory that the appellants breached their duty by filing an allegedly frivolous lawsuit against her, because she had not substantiated that the lawsuit was frivolous. The elements quoted are Sheley's restatement, citing Oasis West Realty, LLC v. Goldman (2011) 51 Cal.4th 811, which was not independently fetched. CourtListener carries two texts of Sheley: a plain-text slip opinion and an HTML text derived from the official reporter, which carries the reporter's page breaks (the quoted passages fall on page 1171). The two differ in one punctuation mark at the elements passage — the slip-opinion text reads "are: (1)" with a colon, the reporter-derived text reads "are (1)" without one; the quotation below follows the reporter-derived text and the discrepancy is disclosed here rather than silently normalized. Section 309's reliance provisions and its liability-limitation language, and the business judgment rule, are covered by this project's Director's Duty of Care and the Business Judgment Rule document rather than here.

THE REMEDY FASHIONED IN JONES: PLACING THE MINORITY IN A POSITION AT LEAST AS FAVORABLE AS THE MAJORITY'S
Jones also addressed what relief would follow if the plaintiff proved her allegations. The court reasoned that the majority's scheme could reasonably be foreseen to destroy the potential public market for the association's stock, depriving the minority of the chance to realize value above book value, and that receipt of an appraised value reflecting book value and earnings alone could not compensate the minority for that loss. Treating the damage as real though its amount was speculative, the court held that equity demands that the minority stockholders be placed in a position at least as favorable as that the majority created for themselves. Concretely, it directed that if the plaintiff proved facts in conformity with her allegations, then upon tendering her shares she would be entitled, at her election, either to the appraised value of her shares on the date of the majority's exchange with interest, or to a sum equivalent to the fair market value of the block of holding-company shares the majority had received for each association share, plus the per-share return of capital the majority had received, with interest — reduced by the amount by which dividends paid on the association's shares in the interim exceeded those paid on a corresponding block of holding-company shares. The court drew an analogy to the statutory appraisal remedy available to shareholders dissenting from a merger, observing that the plaintiff "was entitled to no less" than such protection, "[b]ut she was entitled to more."

STATUTORY BACKDROP: "PERSISTENT UNFAIRNESS" BY THOSE IN CONTROL AS A GROUND FOR INVOLUNTARY DISSOLUTION
Separately from the case-law duty, the General Corporation Law lists conduct by "those in control of the corporation" among the statutory grounds on which a court may order a corporation's involuntary dissolution. Corporations Code § 1800(b)(4) makes it a ground for involuntary dissolution that those in control have been guilty of, or have knowingly countenanced, persistent and pervasive fraud, mismanagement or abuse of authority, or persistent unfairness toward any shareholders, or that the corporation's property is being misapplied or wasted by its directors or officers. Section 1800(b)(5) adds, for corporations with 35 or fewer shareholders, the ground that liquidation is reasonably necessary for the protection of the rights or interests of the complaining shareholder or shareholders. Standing to file such a complaint is limited by § 1800(a): among others, shareholders holding at least one-third of the outstanding shares (or of the outstanding common shares, or of the equity) may file, with the statute excluding from that count shares owned by persons who personally participated in the transactions enumerated in subdivision (b)(4), and any shareholder of a statutory close corporation may file. The statute thus supplies a distinct, equitable remedy directed at the same kind of conduct the Jones duty addresses, alongside the damages and other relief available in an individual or derivative action.

This information sheet relates to Acme Widgets, Inc., a corporation organized under the laws of California, and to Jordan Lee's status as a shareholder of Acme Widgets, Inc. It describes the fiduciary duty that California case law imposes on majority or controlling shareholders of a corporation toward the minority shareholders and the corporation itself — the rule announced by the California Supreme Court in Jones v. H. F. Ahmanson & Co. (1969) 1 Cal.3d 93 — together with the "inherent fairness" standard that accompanies it, the distinction the same decision drew between a minority shareholder's individual claim and a derivative claim brought on the corporation's behalf, later Court of Appeal decisions applying that distinction, and the statutory backdrop in Corporations Code §§ 309 and 1800. Transaction or conduct this information sheet may relate to, if applicable: officer compensation increases approved by the two majority shareholders.

This information sheet is about the duty owed by those who control a corporation through their share ownership, acting singly or together. It is distinct from several other documents in this project: the Director's Duty of Care and the Business Judgment Rule document, which covers the standard of conduct Corporations Code § 309 sets for directors as such; the Self-Dealing and Interested Director/Officer Transactions document, which covers the statutory approval procedures of Corporations Code § 310; the Shareholder Derivative Lawsuit document, which covers the procedural conditions Corporations Code § 800 places on suits brought in the corporation's right; the Involuntary Dissolution of a Corporation document, which covers the dissolution remedy of Corporations Code §§ 1800-1809 in depth; and the LLC Member and Manager Fiduciary Duties document, which covers the statutory duties of Corporations Code § 17704.09 for limited liability companies rather than corporations.

This information sheet is educational only. It does not itself constitute a complaint, a demand, or any other filing; does not determine whether any person is a "controlling" shareholder of Acme Widgets, Inc., whether any particular transaction or course of conduct breached a duty described below, whether a claim would be individual or derivative in character, or what remedy, if any, a court would order; and does not constitute legal advice.

In Jones v. H. F. Ahmanson & Co. (1969) 1 Cal.3d 93, the California Supreme Court rejected the defendants' position that shareholders, as shareholders, owe no fiduciary obligation to other shareholders absent reliance on inside information, use of corporate assets, or fraud — describing that view as one "long been repudiated in California." The court stated the governing rule in two parts. First, majority shareholders, whether acting singly or in concert to accomplish a joint purpose, have a fiduciary responsibility both to the minority and to the corporation to use their ability to control the corporation in a fair, just, and equitable manner. Second, majority shareholders may not use their power to control corporate activities to benefit themselves alone or in a manner detrimental to the minority; any use to which they put the corporation, or their power to control it, must benefit all shareholders proportionately and must not conflict with the proper conduct of the corporation's business. The opinion uses the terms "majority" and "controlling" shareholders interchangeably in stating the duty, and frames it as a duty arising from the ability to control the corporation. Later published Court of Appeal decisions — Jara v. Suprema Meats, Inc. (2004) 121 Cal.App.4th 1238 and Sheley v. Harrop (2017) 9 Cal.App.5th 1147 — quote and apply this same formulation as the settled statement of the duty, with Jara observing that the parties before it did not question "the basic principle of the fiduciary duty owed by majority shareholders to minority shareholders."

The two Court of Appeal decisions cited here quote Jones's formulation verbatim rather than independently restating it, so they corroborate that the Jones formulation remains the operative rule but are not independent sources for its wording. expectedJSON.body: Jones describes the standard that has developed in California as "a comprehensive rule of 'inherent fairness from the viewpoint of the corporation and those interested therein,'" quoting the Court of Appeal's earlier decision in Remillard Brick Co. v. Remillard-Dandini Co. (1952) 109 Cal.App.2d 405. Jones reproduces at length the passage from Remillard — itself quoting the United States Supreme Court's decision in Pepper v. Litton — that the Court of Appeal had declared to be "the law of California": a dominant or controlling stockholder or group of stockholders, like a director, is a fiduciary whose powers are powers of trust; their dealings with the corporation are subjected to rigorous scrutiny; where any of their contracts or engagements with the corporation is challenged, the burden is on the director or stockholder not only to prove the good faith of the transaction but also to show its inherent fairness from the viewpoint of the corporation and those interested in it; and the essence of the test is whether, under all the circumstances, the transaction carries the earmarks of an arm's length bargain, failing which equity will set it aside. Jones adds that Remillard "clearly indicated that the fiduciary obligations of directors and shareholders are neither limited to specific statutory duties and avoidance of fraudulent practices nor are they owed solely to the corporation to the exclusion of other shareholders."

expectedJSON.body: Jones states that the inherent-fairness rule "applies alike to officers, directors, and controlling shareholders in the exercise of powers that are theirs by virtue of their position and to transactions wherein controlling shareholders seek to gain an advantage in the sale or transfer or use of their controlling block of shares." Two consequences follow in the opinion. First, powers that a statute ostensibly grants to majority shareholders remain subject to equitable limitations in favor of the minority: Jones recounts the court's earlier holding in In re Security Finance Co. (1957) 49 Cal.2d 370 that majority shareholders do not have an absolute right to dissolve a corporation, even though the then-governing statute permitted a majority to do so, because that statutory power is subject to equitable limitations — the majority could dissolve to protect their investment only if no alternative means were available and no advantage was secured over other shareholders. Second, the duty reaches a controlling shareholder's dealings in its own shares, not only its votes and management of the corporation: the opinion rejects the defendants' argument that in the use of their own shares they owed no duty to the minority, and holds that a sale or exchange of a controlling block is subject to close scrutiny — where the majority receives a premium over market value for its shares, the consideration for which that premium is paid will be examined, and if it reflects payment for what is properly a corporate asset, all shareholders may demand to share proportionately. Jones also observes that the traditional theories had failed to afford adequate protection to minority shareholders, "particularly to those in closely held corporations whose disadvantageous and often precarious position renders them particularly vulnerable to the vagaries of the majority."

expectedJSON.body: The Jones plaintiff owned 25 of the 6,568 outstanding shares of a California savings and loan association whose stock had no public market. The majority shareholders formed a holding company, exchanged their association shares for holding-company shares without offering the minority the same opportunity, took the holding company public — with a large part of the offering proceeds returned to themselves as capital — and pledged the association's assets and earnings to secure debt incurred for their own benefit; the association then curtailed extra dividends and the holding company offered to exchange the minority's shares on terms far below what the majority had received. On those alleged facts, the court held that the complaint stated a cause of action for breach of the majority's fiduciary duty. The court was explicit about the limits of its holding: it did not suggest that corporate fiduciaries are obligated in all cases to make a market for the corporation's stock, but held that where no market exists, controlling shareholders may not use their control for the purpose of promoting a marketing scheme that benefits themselves alone to the detriment of the minority. Nor did the court suggest that a control block may not be sold or transferred to a holding company; it decided only that the circumstances of any transfer of controlling shares are subject to judicial scrutiny when it appears the controlling shareholders may have breached their fiduciary obligation to the corporation or the remaining shareholders. The opinion notes that alternatives were available to the defendants that would have benefited all stockholders proportionately.

expectedJSON.body: Before reaching the merits, Jones addressed whether a minority shareholder complaining of the majority's conduct must sue derivatively — in the corporation's right, subject to the procedural conditions that govern derivative suits — or may sue in her own name. The court adopted a test keyed to the gravamen of the complaint: an action is derivative if the gravamen is injury to the corporation, or to the whole body of its stock and property without any severance or distribution among individual holders, or if it seeks to recover assets for the corporation or to prevent the dissipation of its assets. By contrast, a shareholder's individual suit enforces a right the shareholder possesses as an individual. Applying that test, the court held the Jones plaintiff's claim was individual: although she alleged that the value of her stock had been diminished, she did not contend that the diminished value reflected an injury to the corporation, so the gravamen of her claim was injury to herself and the other minority stockholders. The court disapproved the earlier Court of Appeal rule of Shaw v. Empire Savings & Loan Assn. that an individual action required an injury different from that suffered by other minority shareholders, holding that the individual wrong need not be unique to the plaintiff, that the same injury may affect a substantial number of shareholders, and that an individual cause of action exists if the injury is not incidental to an injury to the corporation.

expectedJSON.body: In Jara v. Suprema Meats, Inc. (2004) 121 Cal.App.4th 1238, the Court of Appeal applied the Jones test to a three-shareholder corporation in which the two majority shareholders, who were also its only officers and directors, paid themselves compensation the minority shareholder alleged was excessive. The trial court had treated the claim as one for injury to the corporation that could be pursued only derivatively. The Court of Appeal reversed. Surveying the post-Jones decisions, it read Jones as allowing a minority shareholder to bring a personal action alleging that the majority's breach of fiduciary duty resulted in the majority retaining a disproportionate share of the corporation's ongoing value, and found that the gravamen of the plaintiff's complaint — that he was deprived of a fair share of the corporation's profits by the defendants' generous payment of executive compensation to themselves, which one defendant conceded was done to reduce the profit that had to be shared with the plaintiff — was an injury to him as an individual. The court also explained why the policies behind requiring a derivative action (avoiding multiple suits and unequal treatment of shareholders, encouraging intracorporate resolution, and protecting creditors) had little or no application where there was only one minority shareholder, the defendants were the entire board and all the officers, and the corporation remained a viable business. Jara contrasted this with mismanagement claims: it described Nelson v. Anderson (1999) 72 Cal.App.4th 111, a two-shareholder corporation, as holding that the minority shareholder had no standing to sue the majority shareholder for mismanagement, which had to be pursued through a derivative action.

Harrop (2017) 9 Cal.App.5th 1147, a 25-percent shareholder cross-complained against the two shareholders who together held the other 75 percent and served as the corporation's directors. The Court of Appeal, restating the general elements, identified a claim for breach of fiduciary duty as requiring (1) the existence of a fiduciary relationship, (2) breach of the duty, and (3) damages. On the first element, the court found — quoting the Jones formulation by way of Jara — that the appellants owed the respondent a fiduciary duty in their capacities as majority shareholders and directors of the corporation. The decision illustrates that when the same persons hold a controlling block and also sit on the board, two distinct sources of duty operate at once: the case-law duty of controlling shareholders described in this information sheet, and the statutory standard of conduct for directors in Corporations Code § 309(a), which requires a director to perform the duties of a director in good faith, in a manner the director believes to be in the best interests of the corporation and its shareholders, and with the care, including reasonable inquiry, that an ordinarily prudent person in a like position would use under similar circumstances.

expectedJSON.body: Jones also addressed what relief would follow if the plaintiff proved her allegations. The court reasoned that the majority's scheme could reasonably be foreseen to destroy the potential public market for the association's stock, depriving the minority of the chance to realize value above book value, and that receipt of an appraised value reflecting book value and earnings alone could not compensate the minority for that loss. Treating the damage as real though its amount was speculative, the court held that equity demands that the minority stockholders be placed in a position at least as favorable as that the majority created for themselves. Concretely, it directed that if the plaintiff proved facts in conformity with her allegations, then upon tendering her shares she would be entitled, at her election, either to the appraised value of her shares on the date of the majority's exchange with interest, or to a sum equivalent to the fair market value of the block of holding-company shares the majority had received for each association share, plus the per-share return of capital the majority had received, with interest — reduced by the amount by which dividends paid on the association's shares in the interim exceeded those paid on a corresponding block of holding-company shares. The court drew an analogy to the statutory appraisal remedy available to shareholders dissenting from a merger, observing that the plaintiff "was entitled to no less" than such protection, "[b]ut she was entitled to more."

citations.quote: If, after the trial of the cause, plaintiff has established facts in conformity with the allegations of the complaint and stipulation, then upon tender of her Association stock to defendants she will be entitled to receive at her election either the appraised value of her shares on the date of the exchange, May 14, 1959, with interest at 7 percent a year from the date of this action, or a sum equivalent to the fair market value of a "derived block" of United Financial stock on the date of this action with interest thereon from that date, and the sum of $927.50 (the return of capital paid to the original United Financial shareholders) with interest thereon from the date United Financial first made such payments to its original shareholders, for each share tendered.

expectedJSON.gap: The remedy in Jones was tailored to the specific holding-company exchange before the court and was framed as the relief the plaintiff would receive if she established the alleged facts at trial; the opinion does not announce a general measure of damages for every breach of a controlling shareholder's duty, and the specific figures (a 7 percent interest rate, a $927.50 return of capital, and the May 14, 1959 valuation date) are artifacts of that case. The dissenters' rights provisions Jones analogized to were the former Corporations Code sections then in force; the current provisions (Corporations Code §§ 1300-1313) are covered by this project's Dissenters' Rights document. The two short quotations in the last sentence of the body ("was entitled to no less" and "[b]ut she was entitled to more") are from page 117 of the opinion, where the reporter's headnote marker "(19a)" precedes them; they are paraphrased in context above rather than reproduced as separate citation quotes. This document does not calculate or predict any remedy.

expectedJSON.body: Separately from the case-law duty, the General Corporation Law lists conduct by "those in control of the corporation" among the statutory grounds on which a court may order a corporation's involuntary dissolution. Corporations Code § 1800(b)(4) makes it a ground for involuntary dissolution that those in control have been guilty of, or have knowingly countenanced, persistent and pervasive fraud, mismanagement or abuse of authority, or persistent unfairness toward any shareholders, or that the corporation's property is being misapplied or wasted by its directors or officers. Section 1800(b)(5) adds, for corporations with 35 or fewer shareholders, the ground that liquidation is reasonably necessary for the protection of the rights or interests of the complaining shareholder or shareholders. Standing to file such a complaint is limited by § 1800(a): among others, shareholders holding at least one-third of the outstanding shares (or of the outstanding common shares, or of the equity) may file, with the statute excluding from that count shares owned by persons who personally participated in the transactions enumerated in subdivision (b)(4), and any shareholder of a statutory close corporation may file. The statute thus supplies a distinct, equitable remedy directed at the same kind of conduct the Jones duty addresses, alongside the damages and other relief available in an individual or derivative action.

expectedJSON.gap: The one-third standing threshold is stated in § 1800(a)(2) as "33 1/3 percent"; the fetched leginfo page renders the fraction with typographic spacing ("33 1 / 3 percent"), so that subdivision is paraphrased in the body rather than quoted. Section 1800 is quoted only for its subdivision (b)(4) and (b)(5) grounds; the remaining grounds, the intervention rule of subdivision (c), the court's procedures, and the § 2000 buyout alternative that lets the other shareholders avoid dissolution by purchasing the moving parties' shares are covered by this project's Involuntary Dissolution of a Corporation document. The statute's terms "persistent unfairness" and "those in control" are not defined in § 1800's own text, and no case law construing those terms was fetched for this document. This document does not determine whether any statutory ground or standing requirement is met for any specific corporation.
